extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in complex analysis and algebraic geometry (Riemann surfaces, plane curves)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, propositions, and canonical criteria for meromorphic/holomorphic maps, multiplicity/degree, affine and projective plane curves, divisors and L(D) spaces, differential forms, and the Riemann–Roch theorem for compact Riemann surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sphere as C with a point at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret C∞ as C with a single point ∞ added; topologically, sequences {z_i} in C with |z_i|→+∞ correspond to the point ∞ in C∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use charts (example notation: ϕ1 identifying C∞ \ {N} with C) to view C∞ as compactification of C; intuitive consequence: 'plugging in the hole at ∞' removes a singularity for meromorphic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence meromorphic functions ↔ holomorphic maps to C∞ (Prop 48.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a one-to-one correspondence between meromorphic functions f:X→C and holomorphic maps g:X→C∞ that are not identically ∞: send poles to the point ∞ and ordinary values to C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given meromorphic f, define g(z)=f(z) if f(z)≠∞, and g(z)=∞ if f(z)=∞; check continuity and analyticity at points mapped to ∞ by reparametrizing via t=1/z in local charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of meromorphic functions to be analytic at poles
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is meromorphic on X and extended to g:X→C∞ by mapping poles to ∞, then g is analytic (holomorphic) also at points where f had poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work in local charts around such points and use change of coordinate t=1/z to verify analyticity; this removes singularities by working with C∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a nonconstant holomorphic map between compact Riemann surfaces (Prop 48.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X,Y be compact and f:X→Y holomorphic nonconstant. For each y∈Y, define d_y as the total multiplicity of points in f^{-1}(y). Then d_y is well-defined and constant; this constant is deg(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret deg(f) as the (counted-with-multiplicity) number of preimages of a typical value; locally f looks like z↦z^n, so counting multiplicities makes d_y locally constant and hence constant on connected Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: degree of z↦z^k is k
rubrics_metrics.description: When z↦z^k is extended to C∞→C∞, its degree is k: generic fibers have k distinct preimages, while special fibers have fewer preimages but with multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use k-th roots for t≠0 and note multiplicity at t=0; this illustrates degree counting multiplicity rather than naive cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local form and multiplicity of a holomorphic map at a point (Prop 48.4.2 & Def 48.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonconstant holomorphic map f:X→Y at p∈X there exists a unique integer m≥1 such that in suitable local charts the induced map is z↦z^m. This m is the multiplicity mult_p(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity m is determined by the lowest nonzero term in the Taylor expansion in local coordinates; multiplicity is invariant under analytic reparametrization of source/target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramification and branch points (Def 48.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A point p with mult_p(f)>1 is called a ramification point; its image f(p) is called a branch point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ramification captures where a covering/map locally fails to be an isomorphism; many points of a nonconstant map have multiplicity 1, ramification points are special.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of orders of a meromorphic function on a compact Riemann surface equals zero (Prop 48.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on a compact Riemann surface X. Then the sum over all points p of ord_p(f) equals 0 (sum of zeros-count minus poles-count = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret by extending f to X→C∞ and comparing multiplicities in fibers of 0 and ∞; example computations show zeros counted with multiplicity equal poles counted with multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity theorem for holomorphic maps between Riemann surfaces (Thm 48.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g:X→Y are holomorphic maps and f=g on a nonempty open subset of connected X, then f=g everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holomorphic maps are rigid: local agreement on an open set forces global equality; connectivity of X is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsingularity criterion for affine plane curve points (Thm 49.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X defined by polynomial f(x,y)=0, a point (x,y)∈X is smooth (nonsingular) if not both partial derivatives ∂f/∂x and ∂f/∂y vanish at (x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ∂f/∂x≠0 (resp. ∂f/∂y≠0) near a point, X can be locally parametrized as x=g(y) (resp. y=h(x)) by the implicit function theorem; singularities occur exactly where the gradient vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex charts on affine plane curves via projection (Def 49.1.5 and surrounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an affine plane curve X={(z,w)∈C^2: f(z,w)=0} that is connected and smooth, complex charts are given by projecting: where ∂f/∂z≠0 use ϕ(z,w)=w, where ∂f/∂w≠0 use ϕ(z,w)=z, producing a Riemann surface structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction gives local coordinates and defines the analytic structure on X; the charts are chosen on open sets where the corresponding partial derivative does not vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectedness + smoothness ⇒ affine plane curve is a Riemann surface (Def 49.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X={f=0} in C^2 is connected and smooth at every point (gradient nonzero everywhere on X), then X is a Riemann surface (1-dimensional complex manifold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The given chart construction is natural/universal: maps into/out of X are analytic iff compositions with inclusion/projection are analytic; connectedness ensures X is a single Riemann surface rather than disconnected pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness criterion for projective plane curves: homogeneity of polynomial (Sec 49.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a projective plane curve X⊆CP^2 by f(x,y,z)=0 one requires f to be homogeneous so that the notion f=0 is well-defined on projective equivalence classes (x,y,z)∼(λx,λy,λz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use projective charts (ϕ0,ϕ1,ϕ2) to identify intersections with affine charts; homogenization of an affine polynomial f(x,y) gives a homogeneous g(x,y,z) restricting to f on an affine chart (e.g., z=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogenization example for elliptic curve (Example 49.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given affine elliptic curve f(x,y)=x^3−x−y^2, homogenize to g(x,y,z)=x^3−xz^2−y^2z so that the projective curve g=0 in CP^2 restricts to f=0 on the affine chart z=1; the resulting curve is compact in CP^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogenization often uses minimal powers of z to make the polynomial homogeneous; different choices (multiplying by higher powers of z) change the homogeneous polynomial but define the same affine chart restriction up to projective embedding considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of differential 1-forms on C (Def 50.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1-form ω on open U⊆C is an expression f(z)dRe + g(z)dIm where f,g are smooth U→C functions (smooth as real 2-variable functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently ω corresponds to a pair of real-valued 1-forms (Re ω, Im ω) by projection; think of dz as the 1-form giving change in complex coordinate z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and integration interpretation of 1-forms (Sec 50.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: At each point ω_p is an R-linear map on the tangent space; visualize ω by a quiver field labeling values for tangent directions. Integrating ω along a curve sums the values corresponding to local tangent directions, e.g., ∫_c dz equals the net change in z along c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This picture helps compute integrals approximately by adding local contributions; examples include dz and d(z^2)=2z·dz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic 1-forms and type (1,0) vs (0,1) (Defs 50.2.5 & 50.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1-form ω is holomorphic on C if ω=f(z)·dz with f holomorphic. A 1-form is type (1,0) if locally of the form f(z)dz for smooth f, and type (0,1) analogously (local form involving d ar z / conjugate-type term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type (1,0) forms satisfy ω_p(e2)=i·ω_p(e1) (rotation by 90° multiplies value by i); holomorphic forms are special type (1,0) forms with f holomorphic. (Text notes the definition is well-defined because holomorphic coordinate changes scale directions uniformly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Order ord_p(f) of a meromorphic function (Def 51.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For meromorphic f at p, ord_p(f)=d if f has a zero of multiplicity d at p; ord_p(f)=−d if f has a pole of order d at p; ord_p(f)=0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This integer-valued local invariant is used to form divisors and to bound allowed poles/zeros when defining spaces L(D) of meromorphic functions with prescribed behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of divisor on a Riemann surface (Def 51.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A divisor D on X is a function D:X→Z which is nonzero only on a discrete (finite if X compact) set of points. Notation: write p for the divisor taking 1 at p and 0 elsewhere; formal sums like ∑ n_p·p represent divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisors encode prescribed zeros/poles; they form an abelian group under addition and scale under integer multiplication. Use notation like (z−i)^{−3}·(z−∞)^{−4} to denote D with D(i)=−3, D(∞)=−4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a divisor (Def 51.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For divisor D on compact X, deg(D) is the sum over p∈X of D(p) (finite sum since support finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree is additive and for principal divisors (div(f)) degree equals 0 (Proposition 51.4.2). Degree is central in Riemann–Roch formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisor of a meromorphic function and principal divisors (Def 51.4.1 & Prop 51.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For meromorphic f, div(f) is the divisor with div(f)(p)=ord_p(f). A divisor equal to div(f) for some f is principal; principal divisors on compact X have degree 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal divisors formalize the zeros/poles of f; this links function theory to divisor arithmetic and shows constraints like total order sum = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial ordering of divisors and definition of L(D) (Defs 51.4.3 & 51.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define D≥0 if D(p)≥0 for all p. For divisors D1,D2 define D1≥D2 iff D1−D2≥0. For divisor D, L(D) = {f meromorphic on X | div(f) ≥ −D}, i.e., meromorphic functions whose poles are bounded by D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L(D) is a finite-dimensional complex vector space for compact X; containment behavior: D1≤D2 ⇒ L(D1) ⊆ L(D2); special cases: L(0)≅C and if deg(D)<0 then L(D)={0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch theorem (Thm 51.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a divisor D on an algebraic curve X of genus g and a canonical divisor K, dim L(D) − dim L(K−D) = deg(D) + 1 − g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental formula relates analytic/geometric invariants (dimensions of spaces of meromorphic functions/sections) to topological invariant g and divisor degree; the canonical divisor K encodes differentials. The text signals intended explanations and applications follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line bundle viewpoint and sections (Sec 52.1 overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: A line bundle π:L→X is a space whose fiber over each point is a (one-dimensional) line; sections generalize functions (a section picks a vector in the fiber over each point). Nontrivial bundles (e.g., Möbius strip) do not admit global trivializing sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line bundles allow operations (tensor product) corresponding to adding 'twists'; they are tightly related to divisors and linear equivalence classes via the Picard group and give geometric interpretation of spaces like L(D).
